content.body: Imagine you're at a fruit stand with two baskets. You can only pick fruits of two types, but you want to collect as many fruits as possible in total. How would you figure out the longest stretch of fruits you can pick? In this lesson, we'll learn an efficient way to solve this using a lookup structure.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why a brute-force approach becomes inefficient for larger arrays.
2. Apply a hash map to track fruit types and their counts.
3. Implement the sliding window technique combined with a hash map to find the maximum fruits.
4. Determine when to add to the hash map versus when to remove from it.
5. Identify what to store as keys (fruit types) and values (counts) in the hash map.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a small example. You have two baskets and this sequence of fruits:
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: What's the longest stretch of fruits you can pick if you can only collect two types?
content.successMessage: Great! You can pick all three fruits: types 1 and 2.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now with more fruits, what's the longest stretch?
content.successMessage: Well done! The longest stretch is 3 fruits: types 1 and 2 (indices 1-3).

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Excellent! You likely checked many windows to find the longest stretch of 5 fruits.

content.body: What you just did was a brute-force approach: you checked every possible starting point and expanded until you had more than two fruit types. This works for small arrays but becomes slow for larger ones.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has thousands of fruits, checking every possible window is inefficient. We need a smarter method that avoids re-scanning. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we have already seen. Instead of starting over for each window, we'll use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to track the fruit types in our current window and their counts. This lets us quickly check if we have more than two types and adjust our window efficiently.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down each fruit type we've picked and how many of each. When we pick a new fruit, we check our notebook to see if we already have that type or if we need to remove some fruits to stay within two types.

content.body: We'll use a sliding window with a hash map. As we move through the array, we add fruits to our map and shrink the window from the left if we have more than two types. This way, we only pass through the array once.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [1,2,1]: Start with empty map and window [1] → map {1:1}. Add 2 → map {1:1, 2:1} (2 types). Add 1 → map {1:2, 2:1} (still 2 types). Max length = 3.
With [0,1,2,2]: Window grows to [0,1,2] → map has 3 types, so shrink from left: remove 0 → map {1:1, 2:1}. Add 2 → map {1:1, 2:2}. Max length = 3.

content.body:
1. Initialize a hash map to store fruit types and their counts in the current window.
2. Use two pointers (left and right) to represent the sliding window.
3. Move the right pointer to add fruits to the map.
4. If the map has more than two keys, move the left pointer to remove fruits until we're back to two types.
5. Keep track of the maximum window size as we go.

steps.instruction: After adding a fruit, check if the map has more than two keys. If so, move the left pointer to remove fruits until we're back to two types.
steps.hint: Use a while (fruitCount.size > 2) loop. Decrease count of fruits[left] and remove if zero, then left++.
steps.expectedOutcome: While loop that shrinks window when fruitCount.size > 2.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're managing the window size smartly.

steps.title: Update maximum fruits
steps.instruction: After ensuring the window has at most two types, update maxFruits with the current window size.
steps.expectedOutcome: maxFruits updated with current window length.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're tracking the best result.

content.body: Congratulations! You've successfully implemented the 'Fruit Into Baskets' algorithm using a hash map and sliding window. Remember: the hash map lets us track what we've seen (fruit types as keys, counts as values), and we check it each step to decide when to shrink the window. This approach runs in O(n) time, much faster than brute force!
